questions.qtext: Which of the following languages is/are not Turing decidable?

options.text: $\text{L}_1:=\{<\mathrm{M}> \mid \mathrm{M}$ is a $\mathrm{\text{TM}}$ that halts on all inputs and $\mathrm{L}(\mathrm{M})=\mathrm{L}^{\prime}$ for some undecidable language $\text{L}’\}.$
$\text{L}_2:=\{<\mathrm{M}>\mid \mathrm{M}$ is a $\text{TM}$, and $\mathrm{M}$ accepts (at least) two strings of different lengths $\}$.
$\text{L}_3:=\{<\mathrm{M}>\mid \mathrm{M}$ is a $\text{TM}$ such that both $\mathrm{L}(\mathrm{M})$ and complement of $\mathrm{L}(\mathrm{M})$ are finite $\}.$

questions.subject: Technical

questions.qtext: Which of the following statements is/are false?

options.text: If a language $\text{L}$ is generated by a context-free grammar that is not a regular grammar, then $\text{L}$ must not be a regular language.
If a language $\text{L}$ is accepted by a nondeterministic finite automaton, then there must be some push-down automaton(PDA) that also accepts $\text{L}.$
If $\text{L, M}$ are two context-free languages, then $\text{L} \cap \text{M}$ is not context-free.
Every nondeterministic PDA can be transformed into an equivalent deterministic PDA.
